import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 587

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/587](https://www.erdosproblems.com/587)
-/

namespace Erdos587

/--
`MaxNotSqSum N` is the size of the largest subset `A` of
`{1,...,N}` such that for all non-empty `S ⊆ A`, the sum
`∑ n ∈ S, n` is not a square.
-/
def MaxNotSqSum (N : ℕ) : ℕ :=
    (Finset.Icc 1 N |>.powerset.filter fun A => ∀ S ⊆ A, S ≠ ⊥ →
      ¬ IsSquare (∑ n ∈ S, n)).sup Finset.card

/--
Nguyen and Vu proved that $|A| \ll N^{1/3} (\log N)^{O(1)}$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_587.variants.nguyen_vu : ∃ᵉ (O > 0) (O' > 0),
    ∀ᶠ N in Filter.atTop, (MaxNotSqSum N : ℝ) ≤ O' * Real.nthRoot 3 N * (N : ℝ).log^O := by
  sorry

end Erdos587

reformulations.difference: Lean takes the unspecified logarithmic exponent to be a positive natural number and expresses the asymptotic estimate as an eventual inequality, with a positive real multiplier, for MaxNotSqSum.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For sufficiently large N, log N ≥ 1. Any real constant exponent r can therefore be replaced by the positive integer k = ⌈r⌉₊ + 1, since (log N)^r ≤ (log N)^k; conversely, a natural exponent is a real constant exponent. The multiplier and eventual quantifier express the uniform asymptotic bound. The finite family defining MaxNotSqSum contains the empty set, so its maximum cardinality is attained, and bounding it is equivalent to bounding every admissible A. Also, Real.nthRoot 3 N equals N^(1/3) for every natural N. These equivalences were proved in /workspace/review/equivalence.lean.

sources_consulted: https://www.erdosproblems.com/587 — status and prose remarks read through https://r.jina.ai/https://www.erdosproblems.com/587 because direct requests were blocked by Cloudflare.

Hoi H. Nguyen and Van H. Vu, Squares in sumsets, arXiv:0811.1311v2, Introduction: definitions of S_A and SF(n), the main polylogarithmic upper bound, and surrounding remarks. LaTeX source read from https://arxiv.org/e-print/0811.1311.
review.notes: Both declarations were checked. MaxNotSqSum matches the primary paper’s extremal function, including the exclusion of empty subset sums. Computation for N = 0,…,10 gives 0,0,1,2,2,3,3,3,4,4,4; the zero and one cases introduce no defect. Maximum attainment, positivity of nonempty subset sums, and the asymptotic reformulation were verified in Lean without relying on the admitted theorem. The source records the Nguyen–Vu result as solved, consistent with the category tag.
